     8	# A value derived from one row is modelled in DAB and computed in the mapping, and arithmetic there is bounded by this record
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	"How many days did they take" is the first number this system reports that does not exist in the
    13	source. Every measure so far has been a count — one per row — or a sum of a single attribute that
    14	was already there. A ship lag is two dates subtracted, and there is no established place to put
    15	the subtraction.
    16	
    17	Three things are already settled and an argument that reopens them has not read the standard.
    18	
    19	**The measure's name and its arithmetic are written down.** Conventions §2's own worked example is
    20	this question:
    21	
    22	> | `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is
    23	> `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive
    24	> measures. |
    25	
    26	So the two measures are named, the division is a question's job, and `ship_lag_orders_days` is a
    27	*stored measure* — a column in the bridge's published contract. That sentence decides more of this
    28	slice than anything else in the repository.
    29	
    30	**An event that did not happen is already decided.** ADR 0002: "A transaction stage reads
    31	`dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest version in which the event's date is set… An unshipped order
    32	therefore has no shipment event *by construction* rather than by a filter somebody has to
    33	remember." The generator emits `WHERE <date> IS NOT NULL` and a test pins it. The 21 unshipped
    34	orders are the case that design was written for, not a new problem.
    35	
    36	**Two events on one entity already work.** The neutral fixture has declared two events on one
    37	entity since slice 1, and generating this slice's bridge from a scratch copy of the model needs
    38	**no generator change at all**. What is new is one thing only: a sum measure with no attribute to
    39	point at.
    40	
    41	## Decision Drivers
    42	
    43	* a number the business reads has exactly one definition, in the one place data is explained
    44	* the acceptance check keeps an arbiter: when two queries disagree, something decides which is wrong
    45	* the precedent this sets is one the next three slices can live with
    46	* a rule the next person inherits, rather than an example they have to interpret
    47	* DAR stays a layer that can be deleted and rebuilt from the model
    48	
    49	## Considered Options
    50	
    51	* **(a)** A `NUMBER` attribute on `ORDER`, computed in the mapping from two columns of its own row
    52	* **(b)** An expression in `dab/uss.yaml`, emitted into the bridge by the generator
    53	* **(c)** Computed in the question's `uss.sql` at query time from two dates on the peripheral
    54	
    55	## Decision Outcome
    56	
    57	Chosen: **(a), a `NUMBER` attribute computed in the mapping** — with the precedent bounded here,
    58	because "M5 permits it" is otherwise the standing argument for whatever M5's regex happens not to
    59	catch.
    60	
    61	It is also the only option that generates today. A `sum` measure must name an attribute the model
    62	declares; `src/adss/uss.py` raises `KeyError: "ORDER has no attribute …"` otherwise, and there is
    63	no `expression:` field on a measure. (b) and (c) are not choices between working designs — they
    64	are proposals to build something.
    65	
    66	**Why not (b).** Putting the arithmetic in the generator is the serious rival, and it is cleaner in
    67	one respect: nothing derived is stored, so nothing derived can drift. It fails on where it leaves
    68	slice 6. A second source that reports elapsed days *directly* has no two dates for a DAR expression
    69	to subtract, so integrating it needs the attribute anyway — and then there are two definitions of
    70	ship lag, a DAB attribute and a DAR expression, differing by source. That is B2 and B8 failing
    71	together in the slice whose entire purpose is to prove B2. It also costs slice 4, where the
    72	expression vocabulary would have to grow from a two-date special case to general arithmetic in the
    73	same slice that first exercises the fan-out property D-0001 is carried on. Two risky things at once.
    74	
    75	A free-text SQL expression in YAML additionally breaks §3 — "SQL that lives in a Python string is
    76	written to a file so the same linter sees it" — because the linter runs on `.sql` files and would
    77	never see it.
    78	
    79	**Why not (c).** Conventions §2 says ratios are not stored and the numerator *is* an additive
    80	measure; (c) reads it as licence for the whole computation and has no `ship_lag_orders_days` at
    81	all. The question could then not declare what it measures: every `defines` entry must resolve to
    82	something the model or the sidecar defines, so "days to ship" would exist in one SQL file and
    83	nowhere else, with the page's own glossary unable to explain the second number it displays.
    84	
    85	The fatal objection is narrower. §6: "When a question's two queries disagree, `dab/model.yaml` is
    86	the arbiter. The query that departs from the definition is the one that changes." Under (c) the
    87	answer query says `date_diff('day', o.placed_on, o.shipped_on)`, the control says
    88	`shipped_date - order_date`, and the model has nothing to say about either. Neither query can
    89	depart from a definition that does not exist, so the repair procedure stops existing in exactly the
    90	slice that introduces the first computed number — and the cheapest repair becomes making the two
    91	queries agree with each other, which deletes the only thing the check measures.
    92	
    93	(c) also computes as of the wrong instant: the peripheral is current state, while a bridge row is
    94	the latest version *in which the event's date is set*. Those coincide today. ADR 0006 records a
    95	review catching precisely this confusion one layer down, and calls the distinction the entire
    96	difference between the option chosen there and the one rejected.
    97	
    98	### The line this record draws
    99	
   100	M5 permits an expression that reads its own row, and its prose enumerated three forms — a column,
   101	a cast, a `CASE` over columns of that row. A subtraction of two dates is none of them, and passes
   102	only because M5's mechanical check is four keywords and seven function names. Relying on that
   103	silently is the quiet exception §11 rules out. So the rule, in force from here:
   104	
   105	> **Arithmetic over columns of the same row is permitted in a mapping.** A `CASE`, a
   106	> default, a coalesce that invents a value, a filter, a bucket, or anything that changes the grain
   107	> is not — those are meaning, and meaning belongs in the model as an attribute with a definition.
   108	
   109	Conventions §1.4 M5 is clarified to say so, per §11's first rung. The distinction is that
   110	arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies; the others produce a value
   111	somebody chose, and a choice needs a definition beside it.
   112	
   113	`CASE` moves to the forbidden side, and the first draft of this record had it on both. M5
   114	permitted "a `CASE` over columns of that row" and the rule above forbade "a `CASE` on *values*" —
   115	but every `CASE` is over columns and on their values at once, so the pair decided nothing and
   116	handed back exactly the argument this section exists to close. By the test above a `CASE` is
   117	always a choice.
   118	
   119	One trap belongs in the record because the error message misleads: `extract(DAY FROM (b - a))` is
   120	**refused** by M5's checker, because the regex matches the bare word `from` inside the expression.
   121	The refusal says the expression "reaches beyond its row", which it does not. `date_diff('day', a,
   122	b)` passes and is what the mapping uses. The false refusal is a defect in the checker, fixed in
   123	this slice.
   124	
   125	## Consequences
   126	
   127	* Good, because the lag has one definition, in the one place the data is explained, and both of the
   128	  question's queries are measured against it
   129	* Good, because a second source that reports the lag directly maps onto the same attribute rather
   130	  than needing a second derivation — which is the slice-6 case that decided this
   131	* Good, because slice 4's revenue follows the same rule without a new mechanism: quantity, price
   132	  and discount are columns of one order line, and their product is arithmetic over that row
   133	* Good, because DAR stays deletable: everything it emits still comes from the model and the sidecar
   134	* Bad, because a derived value is now stored, and a stored derivation can disagree with what it was
   135	  derived from. Nothing today can make that happen — one mapping, one source — and it becomes
   136	  possible in slice 6
   137	* Bad, because the line above is a rule enforced by review. M5's checker cannot tell arithmetic
   138	  from a bucket, and writing a checker that could is a bigger thing than this slice needs
   139	
   140	## Confirmation
   141	
   142	`tests/test_mapping_rules.py` asserts that a same-row function is accepted and that the reaching
   143	forms are still refused, including the `extract(… FROM …)` case that used to be refused for the
   144	wrong reason.
   145	
   146	The two measures are `SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT` and `SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS`, and the ratio appears in no
   147	schema: the question returns both additive measures and the page divides them. That is not only
   148	§2's rule but what keeps the acceptance check exact — every value either query returns is a
   149	`BIGINT` count or an exact `DECIMAL` sum, and the two answers are compared row by row as values.
   150	A float would break that comparison in a way no test would find on the machine that wrote it:
   151	DuckDB's `sum` over doubles is order-dependent, measured here as `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` summing to
   152	`0.6000000000000001` and the same three reversed to `0.6`.
   153	
   154	Two things guard it, and it is worth being exact about which catches what. `tests/test_exactness.py`
   155	pins the predicate — a float is reported, a `Decimal` and a `bool` are not, every row is looked
   156	at, not only the first. That runs on every commit. The predicate is then applied to both answers
   157	of every question by a data check in `run_checks`, which runs after `adss build` rather than in
   158	the gate — so a float-valued measure fails `adss check`, not `pytest`, and it fails on the
   159	*values* returned rather than on a column's declared type.
   160	
   161	What is **not** confirmed, and is recorded rather than claimed: nothing checks that
   162	`SHIP_LAG_DAYS` still equals the two dates it was derived from. Such a check is tautological
   163	today — one mapping computes it from those columns and nothing else writes it — and stops being
   164	tautological in slice 6, which is the slice this decision's one real risk lands in. It is not
   165	written now because a check that cannot fail teaches a reader that the property is guarded when it
   166	is not; slice 6 writes it, against the case that makes it meaningful.

     8	# A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity, so two events on one entity may not name the same measure
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	Slice 3 is the first slice where one entity has two events: an order is both placed and shipped.
    13	That splits two things which have been the same thing until now.
    14	
    15	A measure's **column** and its **glossary token** are keyed on the entity:
    16	
    17	```python
    18	(event, measure, f"_measure__{event.entity_id.lower()}__{measure.id.lower()}")
    19	found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
    20	```
    21	
    22	Its **ownership** is keyed on the event — `_branch` decides which stage carries a value and which
    23	emits a typed null by identity on the event object. So the generator knows exactly which stage owns
    24	a measure, and then names it after something else.
    25	
    26	With one event per entity those keys coincide and nothing can go wrong. With two, declaring the
    27	same measure id on both events of one entity is accepted without a word, and produces:
    28	
    29	- **the same column twice** in the published contract, and
    30	- **one definition silently replacing the other** in the glossary.
    31	
    32	Reproduced on the neutral fixture. The column list came back with
    33	`_measure__parent__happened_parents_count` at two positions, and the glossary held the *second*
    34	event's definition under the first event's token.
    35	
    36	The two halves fail very differently. DuckDB does not refuse two columns of one name — measured,
    37	`CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS a` yields `a` and `a_1` — so the built table's columns would
    38	not match `bridge_columns()` and the contract check would fail the build loudly. That half is safe.
    39	
    40	**The glossary half is caught by nothing.** No check inspects `definitions()`. That dictionary is
    41	what a question's `defines` entries are resolved against, and what the page renders as "What the
    42	words mean". So a question could reference a measure, resolve it successfully, and be shown a
    43	definition belonging to a different measure — on the page a reader accepts the slice on — while
    44	every test and every check passes.
    45	
    46	Nothing enforces the naming convention that would prevent it either. Conventions §2's three-part
    47	pattern is a hard rule, and there is no test anywhere that checks a measure name's shape. The
    48	uniqueness of these columns has rested entirely on a rule enforced by reading.
    49	
    50	## Decision Drivers
    51	
    52	* a definition that is silently replaced is worse than one that is missing: nothing looks wrong
    53	* the failure must be loud where it is invisible, not only where DuckDB happens to complain
    54	* a published column contract two consumers are already written against
    55	* whatever is decided now is cheapest now, with two questions in existence
    56	
    57	## Considered Options
    58	
    59	* Refuse the collision when the declarations are read, and keep the entity in the column name
    60	* Rename the column to `_measure__<event>__<measure>` and the token to `<ENTITY>.<EVENT>.measures.<M>`
    61	* Do nothing, and rely on §2's naming pattern to keep ids distinct
    62	
    63	## Decision Outcome
    64	
    65	Chosen: **refuse the collision when the declarations are read.**
    66	
    67	Two events on one entity may not declare the same measure id. The refusal names both events and
    68	says what would be lost, because the loss is not obvious: a reader who has just been told the
    69	column would be duplicated will think of the column, and the definition is the part nothing else
    70	would catch.
    71	
    72	**Why not rename to the event.** It is more correct in principle — the event is what actually owns
    73	a measure, so the name should say so — and it is the cheapest it will ever be, with only two
    74	questions to update. It is rejected on two counts. It changes a published contract that conventions
    75	§1.3 states as a hard rule and ADR 0002 tabulates, in a slice that has no other reason to touch it.
    76	And §2's descriptor slot already carries the event: `placed_orders_count`, `shipped_orders_count`.
    77	Naming the column for the event too would put it in twice, so the more correct scheme reads worse
    78	in every ordinary case in order to disambiguate one that is now refused outright.
    79	
    80	**Why not do nothing.** §2's pattern makes a collision unlikely, not impossible, and "unlikely" is
    81	the wrong guarantee for a failure whose signature is a page showing a plausible sentence about the
    82	wrong number. Two events on one entity is exactly where the pattern's descriptor slot stops doing
    83	the work — `placed` and `shipped` distinguish the count measures, and nothing forces a third
    84	measure to carry a descriptor at all.
    85	
    86	This follows the shape the repository already uses for the same class of problem: ADR 0006 refuses
    87	two edges that would inherit into one key column, for the same reason and with the same argument
    88	about what DuckDB silently does instead of raising. A generator that cannot emit a correct artefact
    89	should say so rather than emit an ambiguous one.
    90	
    91	## Consequences
    92	
    93	* Good, because the glossary can no longer show one measure's definition under another's name,
    94	  which was the only failure here that nothing would have reported
    95	* Good, because it is a refusal in the same place and the same shape as the one for colliding
    96	  edges, so the two read as one rule rather than two special cases
    97	* Good, because it costs nothing today: no existing declaration collides, and no column moves
    98	* Bad, because it forbids a legitimate-sounding declaration — the same quantity measured at two
    99	  events, deliberately, under one name. That would have to be two measures with two definitions,
   100	  which is more honest but more typing. If a slice ever wants it, the answer is to rename to the
   101	  event, and this record is what it supersedes
   102	* Bad, because the deeper mismatch stays: the generator still names by entity what it owns by
   103	  event. This narrows the consequence to nothing rather than removing the cause
   104	
   105	### A correction to ADR 0002
   106	
   107	The same mismatch makes one sentence of ADR 0002's published column contract false, for the first
   108	time, in this slice. `_stage` is defined there as "the entity this row is a row *of*", and
   109	`_measure__<entity>__<measure>` is described as "non-null only on the owning stage". With two
   110	events on `ORDER` both branches emit `_stage = 'order'`, so all 809 shipped rows share a stage with
   111	the placed rows while carrying a null `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`. The column is
   112	non-null only on the owning **event**, which `_event` names and `_stage` does not. The contract's
   113	behaviour is right; that sentence describing it is not.
   114	
   115	## Confirmation
   116	
   117	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts that two events on one entity declaring one measure id are refused,
   118	and that the same id on two *different* entities is still accepted — which is the case the
   119	refusal must not catch, since `_measure__<entity>__` already distinguishes those.
   120	
   121	A second test asserts that `definitions()` returns one entry per declared measure, counting what
   122	the glossary returns rather than the declarations twice, so a silent overwrite fails on the count
   123	rather than on somebody reading a page carefully. That is the assertion that would have caught
   124	this, and it did not exist.
   125	
   126	Both of these were written wrong the first time and a review caught them, which is worth leaving in
   127	the record: the first named an acceptance case no fixture contained, and the second compared a list
   128	with itself. A Confirmation section that names a test is only as good as what the test actually
   129	constructs, and neither of these could have failed for the reason it was written down for.

     8	# A business question is the unit of delivery, carried as a data file with the two queries that must agree on its answer
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	At the coffee machine, "how were sales last quarter?" works, because both people share years of
    13	context. A dashboard has none of it. The gap between that question and one a data system can
    14	answer is the actual work: an answerable question names its aggregation, its measure, its
    15	dimensions and its time grain, and defines every term that two people might read differently.
    16	
    17	This system delivers in slices, and a slice is accepted on a presentation of one question's
    18	answer. So the question is not documentation *about* the work — it is the specification, the
    19	acceptance test, and the thing the page renders. That makes its format load-bearing in three
    20	directions at once, and it has to satisfy constraints that pull against each other.
    21	
    22	`dab/model.yaml` is the only place the data is explained (B8), so a question may not restate a
    23	definition — but it must carry enough that a reader can answer it without a conversation. The
    24	acceptance test compares two business queries, but no test may contain business vocabulary
    25	(conventions §6). And the check that gives the slice its confidence — computing the answer twice
    26	and requiring agreement — is only worth anything if the two computations are genuinely
    27	independent, which is a property nobody can enforce mechanically.
    28	
    29	## Decision Drivers
    30	
    31	* a question is answerable from the file alone, with no conversation
    32	* definitions are referenced, never restated, and every reference is proved to resolve
    33	* the acceptance test names nothing from the business
    34	* the two queries are independent enough that agreement means something
    35	* the question survives being reprioritised, refined or pivoted, which the methodology expects
    36	
    37	## Considered Options
    38	
    39	* A question directory holding `question.md` plus the two queries as `.sql` files
    40	* A single markdown file with the SQL in fenced blocks
    41	* Questions as test functions in `tests/`
    42	* A recorded expected result committed alongside, with no second query
    43	
    44	## Decision Outcome
    45	
    46	Chosen option: **a directory per question under `docs/questions/NN-<slug>/`, holding
    47	`question.md` and the two queries as `staged.sql` and `uss.sql`.**
    48	
    49	Separate `.sql` files rather than fenced blocks, for a reason that is not aesthetic: `.sql` files
    50	are linted by the same sqlfluff hook as every other statement in the repository, and
    51	[conventions §3](../conventions.md) already refuses to let SQL hide inside a string. A fenced
    52	block is a string. The moment the acceptance queries are exempt from the SQL rules, they become
    53	the least-reviewed SQL in a repository whose whole claim rests on them.
    54	
    55	*The file is a data file, and that is what keeps the test clean.* The runner discovers question
    56	directories, reads the front matter, runs both queries and asserts agreement — naming nothing. A
    57	per-question test *function* would smuggle the vocabulary back in through its own name, so the
    58	runner is parameterised over what it finds.
    59	
    60	*Definitions are referenced by identifier.* The front matter lists the model identifiers the
    61	question depends on, and the prose cites them by token rather than by paraphrase. A machinery test
    62	asserts every token resolves to something `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` defines. When a
    63	question needs a term the model does not define, the question is **blocked** and the model change
    64	comes first — which is not an obstacle but the methodology working: a question the model cannot
    65	answer has found a gap in the model, and finding it is what asking was for.
    66	
    67	### What the two queries actually prove, and what they do not
    68	
    69	This deserves to be stated honestly, because it is easy to oversell.
    70	
    71	The control query computes the answer from `das__staged.<table>__current`, bypassing DAB and DAR
    72	entirely. The other computes it from `dar__uss`. CI asserts they agree row for row.
    73	
    74	What it catches is the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see: that
    75	routing a number through integration and generation *changed it*. Dropped rows from a join, a
    76	multiplied measure, a mis-inherited key, a version collapse that kept the wrong row, an event
    77	filter that excluded more than it meant to — all of these show up as a number that no longer
    78	matches the source.
    79	
    80	What it does not catch is a wrong definition. If the model says an order is placed on its shipped
    81	date, both queries can be written to that and both will be wrong together. Nor does it catch a
    82	failure the staged layer shares — and there is one specific case worth naming: the engine's
    83	duplicate-row defect is invisible in every presentation view, so both queries would agree while
    84	the history quietly corrupted. That is why a separate data check counts the base table directly.
    85	
    86	The risk that the two are written to agree rather than to be right is real and cannot be designed
    87	away. Three things reduce it. The queries read different schemas in different vocabularies, so a
    88	transcription is visible as one. The control query is forbidden from mentioning `dab` or
    89	`dar__uss`, so it cannot consult the answer it is checking. And when they disagree,
    90	`dab/model.yaml` is the named arbiter: the query that departs from the definition is the one that
    91	changes, never both until they match. Without that last rule the cheapest repair is to make the
    92	check agree with itself, which deletes the only thing it was measuring.
    93	
    94	A recorded expected result was the alternative. It is simpler and it catches every regression
    95	exactly — but its first recording is only as right as the query that produced it, and after that
    96	it can only confirm the system still agrees with its own past. It is a regression test, not a
    97	reconciliation, and this layer needs the second.
    98	
    99	### Lifecycle
   100	
   101	`status` is one of `draft`, `red`, `green`, `superseded`. The methodology expects a question to be
   102	validated, refined or pivoted once the business sees real data, and all three are wins — so a
   103	refinement edits the question in place and a pivot supersedes it with a new one, keeping the
   104	original with its status set. What the business asked for before it saw the answer is part of the
   105	record of why the model looks the way it does.
   106	
   107	One question, one slice, one branch, one page. The page reads the question's own `uss.sql`, so the
   108	presentation and the test cannot disagree about what was asked.
   109	
   110	### Consequences
   111	
   112	* Good, because the specification, the acceptance test and the rendered page are one artefact,
   113	  which is what makes the prototype the deliverable rather than a report about it
   114	* Good, because the acceptance queries are linted like all other SQL
   115	* Good, because a question that outruns the model is blocked visibly rather than answered
   116	  approximately
   117	* Bad, because every answer is written twice, which is duplicated effort and a second thing to
   118	  maintain when a definition changes
   119	* Bad, because the control query has a shelf life. It stays writable only while a question needs
   120	  no integration; from the first question spanning two sources, writing it against the staged
   121	  layer means reimplementing DAB inside the check. Slice 6 is where that bill arrives, and this
   122	  record does not pay it
   123	* Bad, because "independent" is a property of how the queries were written and nothing enforces
   124	  it. The arbiter rule limits the damage; it does not prevent the sin
   125	
   126	### Confirmation
   127	
   128	`tests/test_questions.py` asserts every question file parses and every definition token resolves
   129	to the model. `check_question` enforces both halves of the boundary rule — the control query
   130	mentions neither `dab` nor `dar__uss` and *does* read a `__current` view, and the answer query
   131	reads `dar__uss` and reaches past it for nothing — because the page runs the answer query verbatim
   132	and a reach past DAR would render, pass, and be exactly the dependency the flow rules exist to
   133	prevent.
   134	
   135	The declared dimensions are asserted against the **answer** query only. An earlier draft of this
   136	record claimed both; that was wrong, and the check caught it on its first run. The control query
   137	says the same thing in the source's own words, and requiring the same spelling in both would force
   138	one to be written from the other — which is precisely the independence this whole arrangement is
   139	for.
   140	
   141	`adss check` runs both queries against the built warehouse and asserts row-for-row equality. Both
   142	suites name nothing from the business.

     8	# An inherited key is resolved from the raw pairs, as of the observation time of the row that inherits it
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	Slice 1 built a bridge with one entity and no relationships. ADR 0002 asserted that one shared
    13	bridge is safe because keys inherit along many-to-one edges while measures do not, and said in as
    14	many words that the walk had zero edges and the property was asserted rather than exercised. This
    15	slice is the first with an edge: an order is placed by a customer, and the question groups the
    16	freight of an order by the *customer's* country, which exists nowhere on the order.
    17	
    18	So the generator has to get `customer_key` onto an order row. The engine offers four places to get
    19	it from, they do not agree with each other, and the names do not say which is which. A probe built
    20	a two-entity model with one relationship, changed a foreign key, and read every object the engine
    21	produced. It overturned two things ADR 0002 states as fact.
    22	
    23	**The relationship view is a *current* view, not a historical one.** ADR 0002 says reading it would
    24	lose a row whose foreign key changed. That is not what happens. The macro behind
    25	`dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is:
    26	
    27	```sql
    28	rank() OVER (PARTITION BY <SRC>_key, type_key ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC) AS nbr
    29	... WHERE nbr = 1 AND row_st = 'Y'
    30	```
    31	
    32	Partitioned by the child, so the child never drops out — it is re-pointed. After the probe moved
    33	CH1 from P1 to P2, the pair table held both rows with `row_st = 'Y'` and the view held `CH1|P2`
    34	alone. Nothing is lost; the *old* pair is what is lost, for every row of that child, retroactively.
    35	The reason to read the raw pairs is therefore history, not disappearance, and ADR 0002 got the
    36	right answer from the wrong mechanism.
    37	
    38	**`view_<entity>_with_rel` does carry relationship keys — on the target side, and it fans out.**
    39	ADR 0002 says its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`. That is true only for the
    40	relationship's *source* entity. Once an entity is a relationship *target*, its `_with_rel` view
    41	becomes a double left join through the pair macro and gains the source entity's key **and every one
    42	of its attributes**, one row per child. The probe measured the consequence:
    43	`sum(CHILD_AMOUNT)` over `view_PARENT_with_rel` returned 200.75 against a true 150.75. That is a
    44	live fan trap in a view whose name invites exactly the join that springs it.
    45	
    46	**`rank()` is not `row_number()`, so a tie returns both rows.** The probe's CH5 had two parent codes
    47	in one load, so two pair rows shared an `eff_tmstp`, and the relationship view returned CH5 twice.
    48	A child appearing twice in the bridge multiplies its measures — the precise failure the bridge
    49	exists to prevent, arriving from the engine's own view rather than from anything we wrote.
    50	
    51	**The model cannot say that an edge is many-to-one.** This is the finding that decides how the rule
    52	is enforced, and it is settled by the engine's own error rather than inferred: adding
    53	`cardinality:` to a relationship is rejected with *"Valid fields are: name, definition, description,
    54	source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type"*, and that list is the whole grammar. The
    55	one candidate, `type`, is not a cardinality slot — it accepts any string without validation
    56	(`1:N`, `MANY_TO_ONE`, `BOGUS_VALUE` all pass `check model`) and is **dropped on compile**: it does
    57	not appear in the compiled `model.json` and never reaches the engine. Nor is the engine merely
    58	silent about cardinality. It is agnostic by design: it treats a child's parents as a *set*,
    59	aggregating all target keys per `(source key, eff_tmstp)` into a fingerprint and writing a row when
    60	that set changes. Many-to-many is a supported case, not a defect.
    61	
    62	So the generator cannot learn "many-to-one" from the model, and it cannot learn it from the data,
    63	because the data is legitimately allowed to be many-to-many. Something else has to say it.
    64	
    65	## Decision Drivers
    66	
    67	* a measure summed over the bridge is additive at every grain, whatever the model's shape
    68	* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
    69	* the generator reads objects whose behaviour has been observed, never ones whose names suggest it
    70	* a case the design cannot handle fails the build loudly rather than answering a question wrongly
    71	* the walk works for zero edges, one edge and, later, a chain — without a special case per depth
    72	
    73	## Considered Options
    74	
    75	* `dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the engine's ranked relationship view
    76	* `dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the raw pairs plus a relationship name, ranked here
    77	* `dab.<SRC>_<TGT>_x` — the pair table directly, with `dab__meta` for the type key
    78	* `dab.view_<TGT>_with_rel` — the view named as though it were for this
    79	
    80	## Decision Outcome
    81	
    82	Chosen option: **`dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, ranked in the generated SQL as of the child row's own
    83	`_observed_at`, one parent per child, with the tie refused by a data check.**
    84	
    85	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is the raw pair table joined to the engine's metadata to add a `rel_name`
    86	column, with no ranking and no `row_st` filter. That is what makes it the right source: the pairs
    87	arrive unfiltered, and the as-of rule is ours and visible in the generated SQL rather than the
    88	vendor's and hidden in a macro. It also solves a naming problem the pair table has on its own — the
    89	pair table is named `<SRC>_<TGT>_x` from the *entity pair*, not from the relationship, so two
    90	relationships between the same two entities land in one table separated only by a `type_key` whose
    91	meaning lives in `dab__meta.atom_contx_desc`. Filtering on `rel_name` says what is meant; filtering
    92	on `type_key = 1` says nothing and breaks when a second edge is declared.
    93	
    94	**As of `_observed_at`, not as of now.** The stage picks a version of the child; the inherited key
    95	is the one in force when that version was observed. Today the stage always picks the child's latest
    96	version, so this coincides with the current parent and the choice looks free. It is not: it is what
    97	keeps the rule stated at the level of a bridge row rather than at the level of a table, so it
    98	survives a stage that keeps more than the latest version, which is what a snapshot event and a
    99	`_is_current = FALSE` row will both need.
   100	
   101	So the ranking partitions by the inheriting key **and its observation time**, not by the key
   102	alone. A review of this slice caught the first draft doing the latter, which collapses to one
   103	parent per key and would hand every retained version of an entity that same parent — "as of now"
   104	wearing this rule's clothes, and passing every check because today no stage keeps two versions.
   105	The distinction costs one column in a `PARTITION BY` and is the entire difference between the
   106	option chosen here and the one rejected.
   107	
   108	**Exactly one parent per child, and a tie is a build failure.** Since neither the model nor the data
   109	can state the cardinality, it is inferred from the mapping and then pinned. The inference is sound:
   110	M5 already forbids an attribute expression from containing a subquery, an aggregate or a reach into
   111	another table, so a relationship's `target_transformation_expression` reads its own row and is
   112	single-valued per staged row *by construction*. What that does not cover is one key appearing on
   113	several staged rows of a single load, which is exactly how the probe's CH5 acquired two parents at
   114	one instant. So the check is not optional decoration on top of the inference — it is the half of the
   115	argument the inference cannot make.
   116	
   117	The generated SQL uses `row_number()` over `eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC` and then the parent key
   118	itself, so it is deterministic and can never emit two rows for one child. `ver_tmstp` is not a
   119	formality: the engine writes a closing row that shares its predecessor's `eff_tmstp` and is
   120	separated from it only by `ver_tmstp`. Determinism alone would be a silent wrong answer, so a
   121	generated check counts children with more than one open parent at the ranking instant and fails the
   122	build when it is not zero. The two together mean the bad case is loud, and that if the check is ever
   123	ignored the damage is a mis-attributed row rather than a doubled measure. Doubling is worse: it is
   124	invisible in both of a question's acceptance queries if both are written the same way.
   125	
   126	**Only open pairs.** The read filters `row_st = 'Y'`. The engine flips a pair to `'N'` in exactly one
   127	case — the source row disappears from `das__staged`, and `FULL_LOG`'s delete branch closes it — and
   128	it keeps both rows when it does. In this architecture `das__staged` is an append-only view over
   129	parquet, so that should never fire; the filter is there because "should never fire" is not a reason
   130	to read a retracted pair if it ever does.
   131	
   132	`view_<TGT>_with_rel` is refused outright and now for a measured reason rather than an assumed one.
   133	The engine's ranked view is refused because its as-of rule is not ours to state and its `rank()`
   134	can fan out. The pair table is refused because it cannot name the relationship it is carrying.
   135	
   136	**A child with no parent keeps its row and inherits a null key.** The probe's CH6 has no pair row at
   137	all, so the join is a left join. An order the source attributes to nobody is still an order that
   138	was placed, and dropping it would change a count that ADR 0002 already published. Null is not a
   139	member: it groups as itself and the generator invents nothing for it, per conventions §1.3.
   140	
   141	### Corrections to ADR 0002
   142	
   143	ADR 0002 is not superseded — its decision stands and this record extends it. Two of its factual
   144	claims are wrong and are corrected here rather than in place, because what a record was when it was
   145	made is the thing that makes it worth keeping:
   146	
   147	1. "A changed foreign key keeps its row, which reading the relationship view would not have done."
   148	   The relationship view does keep the row. It re-points every one of that child's rows at the new
   149	   parent and erases the old pair, which is a different defect and a worse one, because it is
   150	   invisible.
   151	2. "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship key columns at all; its column list is
   152	   byte-identical to `view_<entity>`." True on the source side only. On the target side it carries
   153	   the source entity's key and attributes, fanned out. **ADR 0004 repeats the same claim** —
   154	   "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship keys despite its name" — and is corrected
   155	   here too, not there.
   156	
   157	A third claim, in this record's own first draft, was corrected a commit later: it was written
   158	from a partial reading of the probe that produced it. What that cost is worth naming, because it
   159	is the failure mode this whole arrangement is meant to catch — the decision it reached was the
   160	one the full report supports, so nothing downstream was wrong, and it was right by luck rather
   161	than by reading. The findings it had missed changed how the decision is *enforced*, not what it
   162	is.
   163	
   164	The check ADR 0002 installed for the second claim asserted it of *every* entity, so it fails the
   165	moment CUSTOMER becomes a relationship target. That is the check working: it was pinning observed
   166	behaviour and the behaviour was mis-observed. It is replaced by one that asserts the real rule —
   167	the source side is unchanged, the target side gains exactly the source entity's columns — which is
   168	a stronger statement than the one it replaces and would have caught this in slice 1 had it been
   169	possible to write then.
   170	
   171	## Consequences
   172	
   173	* Good, because the as-of rule is written in the generated SQL, so a reader of `dar/uss/_bridge.sql`
   174	  can see when the inherited key was true without reading a vendor macro
   175	* Good, because the fan-out the engine's own views expose cannot reach the bridge: the generator
   176	  emits `row_number()`, and the case that would have needed it fails the build first
   177	* Good, because filtering on `rel_name` keeps two edges between the same two entities in
   178	  separate pair objects. It does **not** keep them apart in the bridge, which a review of this
   179	  slice caught: a stage carries one key column per entity it inherits from, so two such edges —
   180	  or an edge from an entity to itself — would emit that column twice under one name, and DuckDB
   181	  resolves the ambiguity instead of raising. The generator refuses both shapes rather than
   182	  emitting them. Naming the column after the edge instead of the target would allow them and
   183	  would change the bridge's published contract, so it is a decision for the slice that first
   184	  needs two, not a shape to guess at now
   185	* Good, because the walk is the same shape at zero edges and one, so slice 5's two-hop chain extends
   186	  it rather than special-cases it
   187	* Bad, because the generated bridge SQL grows a ranked CTE per edge, and at three or four edges it
   188	  stops being readable in one screen. It is generated, linted and drift-checked, so this costs
   189	  legibility rather than correctness
   190	* Bad, because `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is an engine-internal object with no compatibility promise,
   191	  like every other object here. The pinning checks are what turn a vendor change into a failure
   192	  instead of an empty column
   193	* Bad, and not fixable here: **a foreign key set to null is never retracted.** The engine's reader
   194	  filters the pair source on the target key being non-null, so "this child now belongs to nobody" is
   195	  inexpressible — re-landing a child with a null parent writes no row, no tombstone and no `row_st`
   196	  flip, and the stale pair survives forever. The probe reproduced this. If the source ever nulls an
   197	  order's customer, DAB keeps the old customer and nothing says so. That is a property of the
   198	  engine, not of this decision; it is recorded here because this is the decision that would
   199	  otherwise be blamed for it
   200	
   201	## More Information
   202	
   203	The probe found one thing that is not used and should be, when there is a reason to. Every
   204	presentation object wraps a DuckDB table macro taking a `p_eff_tmstp` with a default, so the whole
   205	DAB layer is point-in-time queryable for nothing: `f_child_parent_x(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-15')` returned
   206	the January parent while `f_child_parent_x()` returned the current one. That is a second, shorter
   207	way to write the as-of join. It is not taken because it moves the as-of rule back inside a vendor
   208	macro, which is the thing this decision is spending SQL to avoid — but a later slice that needs
   209	as-of over several objects at once should weigh it again rather than rediscover it.
   210	
   211	`type_key` is not stable across models: it was 1 for the relationship in this probe and 17 in an
   212	earlier one, and attribute type keys differ per entity within a single model. It is never
   213	hardcoded — `rel_name` is what the generated SQL matches on, which is the whole reason
   214	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is read rather than the pair table it wraps.
   215	
   216	## Confirmation
   217	
   218	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts the generated bridge left-joins the pairs rather than inner-joining
   219	them, that it ranks by `row_number` and not `rank`, that the ranking is as of the child's
   220	`_observed_at`, and that a non-owning branch still emits a typed null for a key it does not own —
   221	this last one because a union takes its column names from its first branch, so the order of the key
   222	columns is the invariant and counting them would not catch a transposition.
   223	
   224	A generated data check counts children with more than one parent at the ranking instant and must
   225	return zero. Another counts bridge rows whose inherited key resolves to no row in the target
   226	peripheral, which is the shape a mis-spelled M6 target expression takes: the engine reports nothing
   227	at deploy or at execute, and the column is simply null everywhere.
   228	
   229	The engine-behaviour checks are widened rather than removed: `_focal` and `_idfr` are still empty,
   230	`view_<E>_with_rel` is unchanged on a relationship's source side and gains exactly the source
   231	entity's columns on its target side.
   232	
   233	What this slice still does not prove is the fan-out property itself. Both entities here are at the
   234	same grain — one order has one customer — so no measure can multiply across the edge no matter how
   235	the join is written. The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the
   236	test that a parent's measure is not multiplied by its children becomes possible. Saying so is the
   237	point: ADR 0002 asserted this property in slice 1 and it is still asserted now.

1	# What the generated star schema needs to know that the business model does not otherwise
     2	# say: which date makes an entity a measurement event, and which numbers are its measures.
     3	#
     4	# These are business facts -- "an order is placed on a day, and counting orders means
     5	# counting orders" -- so every one carries its own definition. The glossary copies these
     6	# strings; it never composes one. Names follow docs/conventions.md section 2.
     7	uss:
     8	  events:
     9	    - id: PLACED
    10	      entity: ORDER
    11	      definition: >-
    12	        An order was placed: the business accepted a customer's request and committed to
    13	        supplying it. One per order, on the day it was accepted.
    14	      kind: transaction
    15	      date_attribute: PLACED_ON
    16	      measures:
    17	        - id: PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT
    18	          definition: >-
    19	            The number of orders placed. One for each order, counted on the day the business
    20	            accepted it, regardless of what was on it or whether it was ever delivered.
    21	          aggregate: count
    22	
    23	        - id: FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT
    24	          definition: >-
    25	            What the business paid to have placed orders carried, attributed to the day it
    26	            accepted each one. It is a cost of fulfilment, so it is additive over any set of
    27	            orders and over any period -- but only over orders, since one order carries one
    28	            freight charge however many items are on it.
    29	          aggregate: sum
    30	          attribute: FREIGHT_CHARGE
    31	
    32	    - id: SHIPPED
    33	      entity: ORDER
    34	      definition: >-
    35	        An order shipped: the goods left the business on their way to the destination. One per
    36	        order, on the day they left. An order the business has not recorded as gone has no
    37	        shipment event at all, so it is absent here rather than counted as a zero.
    38	      kind: transaction
    39	      date_attribute: SHIPPED_ON
    40	      measures:
    41	        - id: SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT
    42	          definition: >-
    43	            The number of orders that went out, counted on the day they left rather than the
    44	            day they were accepted. An order accepted in one month and shipped in the next
    45	            counts once, in the second.
    46	          aggregate: count
    47	
    48	        - id: SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS

    51	            orders and any period, because each shipped order contributes its own wait exactly

1	"""The Unified Star Schema, generated: an event bridge, a peripheral per entity, a calendar.
     2	
     3	Keys inherit along many-to-one relationships; measures do not. Copying a parent's measure
     4	onto every child row would multiply it when summed, which is the fan trap a bridge exists to
     5	avoid -- so a measure is non-null only on the stage of the (entity, event) that owns it, and
     6	every other branch of the union emits a typed NULL. ADR 0002.
     7	
     8	Slice 1 has one entity and no relationships, so the walk that inherits keys has no edges. A
     9	zero-edge walk is a valid walk, and the tests say so, because the alternative is meeting it
    10	as a special case the first time an edge exists.
    11	"""
    12	
    13	from __future__ import annotations
    14	
    15	from dataclasses import dataclass
    16	from enum import StrEnum
    17	from pathlib import Path
    18	
    19	import yaml
    20	
    21	from adss.model import Entity, Model, Relationship
    22	from adss.names import Relation, Schema, crossing
    23	
    24	BRIDGE = Relation(Schema.DAR_USS, "_bridge")
    25	CALENDAR = Relation(Schema.DAR_USS, "_calendar")
    26	
    27	COUNT_TYPE = "BIGINT"
    28	SUM_TYPE = "DECIMAL(28, 8)"
    29	
    30	_GENERATED = "-- Generated from dab/model.yaml and dab/uss.yaml. Do not edit; regenerate."
    31	
    32	
    33	class UssError(Exception):
    34	    """A declaration the generator will not build from."""
    35	
    36	
    37	class Aggregate(StrEnum):
    38	    COUNT = "count"
    39	    SUM = "sum"
    40	
    41	
    42	class EventKind(StrEnum):
    43	    TRANSACTION = "transaction"
    44	    SNAPSHOT = "snapshot"
    45	
    46	
    47	@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
    48	class Measure:
    49	    id: str
    50	    definition: str
    51	    aggregate: Aggregate
    52	    attribute_id: str | None
    53	
    54	    @property
    55	    def sql_type(self) -> str:
    56	        return COUNT_TYPE if self.aggregate is Aggregate.COUNT else SUM_TYPE
    57	
    58	
    59	@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
    60	class Event:
    61	    id: str
    62	    entity_id: str
    63	    definition: str
    64	    kind: EventKind
    65	    date_attribute_id: str
    66	    measures: tuple[Measure, ...]
    67	
    68	    @property
    69	    def name(self) -> str:
    70	        return self.id.lower()
    71	
    72	
    73	@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
    74	class Uss:
    75	    path: Path
    76	    events: tuple[Event, ...]
    77	
    78	    def measure_columns(self) -> tuple[tuple[Event, Measure, str], ...]:
    79	        """Every measure column in the bridge, in declaration order."""
    80	        return tuple(
    81	            (event, measure, f"_measure__{event.entity_id.lower()}__{measure.id.lower()}")
    82	            for event in self.events
    83	            for measure in event.measures
    84	        )
    85	
    86	
    87	def read_uss(path: Path, model: Model | None = None) -> Uss:
    88	    """Read the declarations, refusing anything that would generate but should not."""
    89	    document = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text())["uss"]
    90	    events: list[Event] = []
    91	    for declared in document["events"]:
    92	        event_id = str(declared["id"])
    93	        if "definition" not in declared:

    95	                f"{path}: event {event_id} has no definition. A glossary copies these "
    96	                f"strings verbatim, so one that does not exist becomes a blank row."
    97	            )
    98	        measures: list[Measure] = []
    99	        for raw in declared.get("measures", ()):
   100	            aggregate = Aggregate(str(raw["aggregate"]))
   101	            if "definition" not in raw:
   102	                raise UssError(f"{path}: measure {raw['id']} has no definition.")

   106	                    f"{path}: measure {raw['id']} declares aggregate: sum and names nothing "
   107	                    f"to sum. A blank attribute would emit a column named after nothing."
   108	                )

   141	def _refuse_edges_that_would_collide(model: Model) -> None:
   142	    """Two edges into one key column is a silent loss, so it is refused rather than emitted.
   143	
   144	    A stage carries one column per entity it inherits from, named for that entity. Two edges
   145	    from one entity to the same target -- or an edge to the entity itself -- would emit two
   146	    columns of the same name, and DuckDB resolves that ambiguity instead of raising, so one of
   147	    the two inherited keys vanishes with nothing to say which. Distinguishing them means naming
   148	    the column after the edge rather than the target, which changes a published contract, so it
   149	    is a decision for the slice that first needs two such edges rather than a shape to guess at
   150	    now. ADR 0006.
   151	    """
   152	    for entity in model.entities:
   153	        edges = model.edges_from(entity.id)
   154	        for edge in edges:
   155	            if edge.target_entity_id == entity.id:
   156	                raise UssError(
   157	                    f"{edge.id} points at the entity it runs from, so the stage would carry "
   158	                    f"{entity.key_column} twice under one name and lose one of them silently."
   159	                )
   160	        targets = [edge.target_entity_id for edge in edges]
   161	        for target in targets:
   162	            if targets.count(target) > 1:
   163	                colliding = [edge.id for edge in edges if edge.target_entity_id == target]
   164	                raise UssError(
   165	                    f"{' and '.join(colliding)} both inherit into "
   166	                    f"{model.entity(target).key_column}, and a stage carrying that column "
   167	                    f"twice loses one of them with no error. Naming the column after the edge "
   168	                    f"rather than the target would fix it and would change the bridge's "
   169	                    f"published contract, so it is a decision rather than a patch."
   170	                )

   173	def _refuse_measures_that_would_share_a_name(uss: Uss) -> None:
   174	    """Two events on one entity may not declare the same measure id. ADR 0008.
   175	
   176	    A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity. While an entity has one event those
   177	    are the same thing; with two they are not, and the same id on both emits one column twice
   178	    AND silently replaces one definition with the other in the glossary.
   179	
   180	    The column half would fail the build loudly -- DuckDB renames the second column rather than
   181	    raising, so the built table stops matching the published contract. The glossary half is
   182	    caught by nothing: no check inspects the definitions, and they are what a question's
   183	    references resolve against and what the page renders. A reader would be shown a plausible
   184	    sentence about the wrong number, and everything would pass.
   185	    """
   186	    seen: dict[tuple[str, str], str] = {}
   187	    for event in uss.events:
   188	        for measure in event.measures:
   189	            key = (event.entity_id, measure.id)
   190	            if key in seen:
   191	                raise UssError(
   192	                    f"{event.entity_id} declares {measure.id} on both {seen[key]} and "
   193	                    f"{event.id}. A measure is named for its entity and owned by its event, so "
   194	                    f"the two would share one column -- and {event.id}'s definition would "
   195	                    f"replace {seen[key]}'s in the glossary, which nothing checks and the page "
   196	                    f"renders. Give them separate ids, or one definition covering both."
   197	                )
   198	            seen[key] = event.id

   201	def _refuse_measures_of_things_that_are_not_numbers(uss: Uss, model: Model) -> None:
   202	    for event in uss.events:
   203	        if event.kind is not EventKind.TRANSACTION:
   204	            raise UssError(
   205	                f"{event.id} is declared {event.kind}, and the generator only builds "
   206	                f"transaction stages. It would emit a transaction stage anyway and mark "
   207	                f"every row current, which is worse than refusing: nothing downstream could "
   208	                f"tell. A snapshot stage arrives in the slice that first needs one."
   209	            )
   210	        entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
   211	        if not entity.attribute(event.date_attribute_id).is_date:
   212	            raise UssError(
   213	                f"{event.id} is dated by {event.date_attribute_id}, which is not a date."
   214	            )
   215	        for measure in event.measures:
   216	            if measure.attribute_id and not entity.attribute(measure.attribute_id).is_number:
   217	                raise UssError(
   218	                    f"{event.id}.{measure.id} sums {measure.attribute_id}, which is not a "
   219	                    f"number. Summing what is not a number produces a number nobody can read."
   220	                )

   223	def _version_cte(model: Model, event: Event) -> str:
   224	    """The version of each entity this event is measured on: the latest in which it is dated."""
   225	    entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
   226	    date = crossing(event.date_attribute_id)
   227	    held = "revision"
   228	    lines = [
   229	        f"    {held}.{crossing(entity.source_key)} AS {entity.key_column}",
   230	        f"    {held}.eff_tmstp AS _observed_at",
   231	        f"    cast({held}.{date} AS DATE) AS _event_date",
   232	    ]
   233	    for measure in event.measures:
   234	        column = f"_measure__{entity.object_name}__{measure.id.lower()}"
   235	        if measure.aggregate is Aggregate.COUNT:
   236	            value = f"cast(1 AS {COUNT_TYPE})"
   237	        else:
   238	            attribute = crossing(str(measure.attribute_id))
   239	            value = f"cast({held}.{attribute} AS {SUM_TYPE})"
   240	        lines.append(f"    {value} AS {column}")
   241	    selected = ",\n".join(lines)
   242	    return (
   243	        f"{event.name}__version AS (\n"
   244	        f"SELECT\n{selected}\n"
   245	        f'FROM dab."view_{entity.id}_hist" AS {held}\n'
   246	        f"WHERE {held}.{date} IS NOT NULL\n"
   247	        f"QUALIFY row_number() OVER (\n"
   248	        f"    PARTITION BY {held}.{crossing(entity.source_key)}\n"
   249	        f"    ORDER BY {held}.eff_tmstp DESC\n"
   250	        f") = 1\n"
   251	        f")"
   252	    )

   255	def _inherit_cte(model: Model, event: Event, edge: Relationship) -> str:
   256	    """One inherited key: the pair in force when the inheriting row was observed. ADR 0006.
   257	
   258	    Resolved per inheriting ROW rather than per key -- the partition carries the observation
   259	    time -- because that is the whole reason ADR 0006 chose the observation time over "now".
   260	    A stage that kept more than the latest version of an entity would otherwise hand every one
   261	    of those versions the same parent, which is "as of now" wearing the other rule's clothes.
   262	
   263	    Read from `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, which is the raw pairs plus the relationship's name, and
   264	    ranked here rather than by the engine. The engine's own ranked view answers a different
   265	    question -- who the parent is *now* -- and answers it with `rank()`, which returns two rows
   266	    for a child whose source named two parents at one instant. Two rows here would double that
   267	    child's measures, so the ranking is `row_number()` and the tie is refused by a data check.
   268	    """
   269	    source = model.entity(edge.source_entity_id)
   270	    target = model.entity(edge.target_entity_id)
   271	    held = edge.id.lower()
   272	    return (
   273	        f"{event.name}__{held} AS (\n"
   274	        f"SELECT\n"
   275	        f"    revision.{source.key_column} AS {source.key_column},\n"
   276	        f"    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at,\n"
   277	        f"    pair.{crossing(target.source_key)} AS {target.key_column}\n"
   278	        f"FROM {event.name}__version AS revision\n"
   279	        f'LEFT JOIN dab."v_{edge.id}" AS pair\n'
   280	        f"    ON pair.{crossing(source.source_key)} = revision.{source.key_column}\n"
   281	        f"    AND pair.rel_name = '{edge.id}'\n"
   282	        f"    AND pair.row_st = 'Y'\n"
   283	        f"    AND pair.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at\n"
   284	        f"QUALIFY row_number() OVER (\n"
   285	        f"    PARTITION BY revision.{source.key_column}, revision._observed_at\n"
   286	        f"    ORDER BY\n"
   287	        f"        pair.eff_tmstp DESC,\n"
   288	        f"        pair.ver_tmstp DESC,\n"
   289	        f"        pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}\n"
   290	        f") = 1\n"
   291	        f")"
   292	    )

   295	def _stage_cte(model: Model, event: Event) -> str:
   296	    """One stage: the entity's version, with the key of everything it inherits from."""
   297	    entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
   298	    edges = model.edges_from(entity.id)
   299	    lines = [
   300	        f"    revision.{entity.key_column} AS {entity.key_column}",
   301	        "    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at",
   302	        "    revision._event_date AS _event_date",
   303	    ]
   304	    lines += [
   305	        f"    {edge.id.lower()}.{model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column} "
   306	        f"AS {model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column}"
   307	        for edge in edges
   308	    ]
   309	    lines += [
   310	        f"    revision._measure__{entity.object_name}__{measure.id.lower()} "
   311	        f"AS _measure__{entity.object_name}__{measure.id.lower()}"
   312	        for measure in event.measures
   313	    ]
   314	    # One row per inheriting row in each of these, so none of the joins can fan out. LEFT
   315	    # anyway: the row that inherits nothing is kept by the join inside the CTE, and an inner
   316	    # join here would undo that one level up.
   317	    joins = "".join(
   318	        f"\nLEFT JOIN {event.name}__{edge.id.lower()} AS {edge.id.lower()}\n"
   319	        f"    ON {edge.id.lower()}.{entity.key_column} = revision.{entity.key_column}\n"
   320	        f"    AND {edge.id.lower()}._observed_at = revision._observed_at"
   321	        for edge in edges
   322	    )
   323	    selected = ",\n".join(lines)
   324	    return (
   325	        f"{event.name} AS (\nSELECT\n{selected}\nFROM {event.name}__version AS revision{joins}\n)"
   326	    )

   329	def _branch(model: Model, uss: Uss, event: Event, keys: tuple[str, ...]) -> str:
   330	    """One branch of the union: this stage's own columns, and a typed NULL for the rest."""
   331	    entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
   332	    carried = {entity.key_column} | {
   333	        model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column for edge in model.edges_from(entity.id)
   334	    }
   335	    lines = [
   336	        f"    '{entity.object_name}' AS _stage",
   337	        f"    '{event.name}' AS _event",
   338	        f"    {event.name}._event_date AS _event_date",
   339	        "    TRUE AS _is_current",
   340	        f"    {event.name}._observed_at AS _observed_at",
   341	    ]
   342	    for key in keys:
   343	        value = f"{event.name}.{key}" if key in carried else "cast(NULL AS VARCHAR)"
   344	        lines.append(f"    {value} AS {key}")
   345	    owned = {column for candidate, _, column in uss.measure_columns() if candidate is event}
   346	    for _, measure, column in uss.measure_columns():
   347	        value = f"{event.name}.{column}" if column in owned else f"cast(NULL AS {measure.sql_type})"
   348	        lines.append(f"    {value} AS {column}")
   349	    return "SELECT\n" + ",\n".join(lines) + f"\nFROM {event.name} AS {event.name}"

   352	def entity_ids(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> tuple[str, ...]:
   353	    """Every entity the bridge names, in MODEL order: the ones with events, and the ones they
   354	    inherit from. An entity reached only by inheritance still needs a peripheral, or the bridge
   355	    carries a key that joins to nothing.
   356	    """
   357	    touched = {event.entity_id for event in uss.events}
   358	    touched |= {
   359	        edge.target_entity_id for event in uss.events for edge in model.edges_from(event.entity_id)
   360	    }
   361	    return tuple(entity.id for entity in model.entities if entity.id in touched)

   364	def entity_keys(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> tuple[str, ...]:
   365	    """One key column per entity the bridge names, in MODEL order.
   366	
   367	    Model order, not event order: reordering two events in the sidecar is not a model change,
   368	    and it must not rearrange a contract that consumers are written against. The check cannot
   369	    catch that on its own, because it derives what it expects from this same function.
   370	    """
   371	    return tuple(model.entity(entity_id).key_column for entity_id in entity_ids(model, uss))

   374	def bridge_columns(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> tuple[str, ...]:
   375	    """The published column contract, in order.
   376	
   377	    Grouped: the structural columns, then one key per entity in model order, then one column
   378	    per measure in declaration order.
   379	
   380	    That grouping means the contract does NOT only ever grow at the end, and saying otherwise
   381	    would be the more comfortable lie. A new entity appends a key, and because keys precede
   382	    measures, every measure column moves right. An entity inserted in the middle of the model
   383	    moves the keys after it as well. So the model file's own order is part of this contract,
   384	    and nothing here can catch a rearrangement: the check that compares the built bridge to
   385	    this contract derives what it expects from this same function, so both sides move together
   386	    and it passes either way.
   387	
   388	    What makes that tolerable rather than a defect is that nothing reads this table by
   389	    position. Conventions section 3 forbids `SELECT *`, the questions name their columns and
   390	    so does the destination. A consumer that did read positionally would be reading a contract
   391	    this docstring does not offer it. New entities still go at the end, because moving a key
   392	    column is a bigger change than moving a measure. Blueprint B7.
   393	    """
   394	    keys = entity_keys(model, uss)
   395	    structural = ("_stage", "_event", "_event_date", "_is_current", "_observed_at")
   396	    return structural + keys + tuple(column for _, _, column in uss.measure_columns())
   397

   399	def bridge_sql(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> str:
   400	    """One row per measurement event, over every stage the declarations name."""
   401	    keys = entity_keys(model, uss)
   402	    ctes = ",\n\n".join(
   403	        cte
   404	        for event in uss.events
   405	        for cte in (
   406	            _version_cte(model, event),
   407	            *(_inherit_cte(model, event, edge) for edge in model.edges_from(event.entity_id)),
   408	            _stage_cte(model, event),
   409	        )
   410	    )
   411	    branches = "\n\nUNION ALL\n\n".join(_branch(model, uss, event, keys) for event in uss.events)
   412	    return f"{_GENERATED}\nCREATE OR REPLACE TABLE {BRIDGE.sql} AS\nWITH {ctes}\n\n{branches};\n"
   413

   415	def peripheral_sql(model: Model, entity_id: str) -> str:
   416	    """One row per entity instance, current state, key first and attributes as declared."""
   417	    entity: Entity = model.entity(entity_id)
   418	    lines = [
   419	        f"    e.{crossing(entity.source_key)} AS {entity.key_column}",
   420	        "    e.eff_tmstp AS _observed_at",
   421	    ]
   422	    lines += [f"    e.{crossing(a.id)} AS {a.column}" for a in entity.attributes]
   423	    selected = ",\n".join(lines)
   424	    relation = Relation(Schema.DAR_USS, entity.object_name)
   425	    return (
   426	        f"{_GENERATED}\n"
   427	        f"CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE {relation.sql} AS\n"
   428	        f"SELECT\n{selected}\n"
   429	        f'FROM dab."view_{entity.id}_hist" AS e\n'
   430	        f"QUALIFY row_number() OVER (\n"
   431	        f"    PARTITION BY e.{crossing(entity.source_key)}\n"
   432	        f"    ORDER BY e.eff_tmstp DESC\n"
   433	        f") = 1;\n"
   434	    )

   437	def calendar_sql() -> str:
   438	    """Dense and daily across everything the bridge holds. Civil arithmetic only.
   439	
   440	    A calendar containing only the days something happened is not a calendar: a month with
   441	    no events must still appear in a time series. Fiscal periods and holidays are business
   442	    meaning and would need a definition, so they belong in the model, not in a generator.
   443	    """
   444	    return (
   445	        f"{_GENERATED}\n"
   446	        f"CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE {CALENDAR.sql} AS\n"
   447	        f"WITH bounds AS (\n"
   448	        f"SELECT\n"
   449	        f"    min(b._event_date) AS first_date,\n"
   450	        f"    max(b._event_date) AS last_date\n"
   451	        f"FROM {BRIDGE.sql} AS b\n"
   452	        f"),\n\n"
   453	        f"every_day AS (\n"
   454	        f"SELECT\n"
   455	        f"    cast(d.day AS DATE) AS date_key\n"
   456	        f"FROM bounds AS bo\n"
   457	        f"CROSS JOIN range(\n"
   458	        f"    bo.first_date, bo.last_date + INTERVAL 1 DAY, INTERVAL 1 DAY\n"
   459	        f") AS d (day)\n"
   460	        f")\n\n"
   461	        f"SELECT\n"
   462	        f"    d.date_key AS date_key,\n"
   463	        f"    cast(year(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS year_number,\n"
   464	        f"    cast(quarter(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS quarter_of_year,\n"
   465	        f"    cast(month(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS month_of_year,\n"
   466	        f"    cast(day(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS day_of_month,\n"
   467	        f"    cast(date_trunc('year', d.date_key) AS DATE) AS year_start,\n"
   468	        f"    cast(date_trunc('quarter', d.date_key) AS DATE) AS quarter_start,\n"
   469	        f"    cast(date_trunc('month', d.date_key) AS DATE) AS month_start,\n"
   470	        f"    strftime(d.date_key, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(d.date_key) AS VARCHAR) "
   471	        f"AS quarter_label,\n"
   472	        f"    strftime(d.date_key, '%Y-%m') AS month_label\n"
   473	        f"FROM every_day AS d;\n"
   474	    )

   477	def definitions(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> dict[str, str]:
   478	    """Every definition, by the token that refers to it. Copied verbatim, never composed.
   479	
   480	    A generator that composed a definition would be a third place the data is explained,
   481	    and the worst kind: one nobody wrote and nobody reviews.
   482	    """
   483	    found = dict(model.definitions())
   484	    for event in uss.events:
   485	        found[f"{event.entity_id}.events.{event.id}"] = event.definition
   486	        for measure in event.measures:
   487	            found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
   488	    return found

   202	def reaching(expression: str) -> bool:
   203	    """Whether an expression leaves the row it is written on. M5.

   213	def _without_keyword_from(expression: str) -> str:
   214	    """The expression with the syntactic FROM of each such function blanked, and nothing else.
   215	
   216	    Only that one token, and only when it is genuinely inside the call. An earlier version
   217	    discarded the whole argument list, which excused the very thing M5 exists to stop: a
   218	    subquery hidden in `extract(DAY FROM (SELECT ...))` became invisible. Taking simply the
   219	    next FROM instead was no better -- in `trim(a) FROM elsewhere` the next one is the reach.
   220	
   221	    So the scan finds the first FROM at the call's own bracket depth, and gives up at the
   222	    bracket that closes the call. It steps over single-quoted text, because a bracket inside a
   223	    string literal is not a bracket, and a scan that believed otherwise would run off the end
   224	    and hand the checker half an expression to judge.
   225	    """
   226	    out = expression
   227	    for call in _KEYWORD_FROM.finditer(expression):
   228	        found = _syntactic_from(out, call.end())
   229	        if found is not None:
   230	            out = out[:found] + " " * 4 + out[found + 4 :]

   234	def _syntactic_from(expression: str, opened: int) -> int | None:
   235	    """Where the FROM belonging to a call that opened at `opened` starts, if it has one."""
   236	    depth, index = 1, opened
   237	    while index < len(expression):
   238	        character = expression[index]
   239	        if character == "'":
   240	            closing = expression.find("'", index + 1)
   241	            index = len(expression) if closing == -1 else closing + 1
   242	            continue
   243	        depth += (character == "(") - (character == ")")
   244	        if depth == 0:
   245	            return None
   246	        if (
   247	            depth == 1
   248	            and expression[index : index + 4].lower() == "from"
   249	            and not expression[index - 1 : index].isalnum()
   250	            and not expression[index + 4 : index + 5].isalnum()
   251	        ):
   252	            return index
   253	        index += 1
   254	    return None

   257	def key_shape(expression: str) -> str:
   258	    """A key expression with its column names removed, which is what M6 compares.
   259	
   260	    M6 asks that a relationship's target expression mirror the target entity's own key
   261	    expression. It is the *shape* that has to match, not the spelling: a foreign key column is
   262	    routinely named differently from the primary key it points at. What must not differ is the
   263	    casting, because that is what decides the VARCHAR the two sides produce -- a bare column on
   264	    one side and a cast on the other join to nothing at all.
   265	    """
   266	    parts: list[str] = []
   267	    last = 0
   268	    for literal in _LITERAL.finditer(expression):
   269	        # A separator inside a concat is part of the shape and survives verbatim: 'A1' + '23'
   270	        # and 'A12' + '3' are one key without it.
   271	        parts.append(_without_names(expression[last : literal.start()]))
   272	        parts.append(literal.group(0))
   273	        last = literal.end()
   274	    parts.append(_without_names(expression[last:]))
   275	    return " ".join("".join(parts).split())

   278	def _without_names(fragment: str) -> str:
   279	    def anonymous(word: re.Match[str]) -> str:
   280	        found = word.group(0).lower()
   281	        if found in _SHAPE_WORDS:
   282	            return found
   283	        # A name immediately followed by "(" is a function, and a function decides the value
   284	        # as surely as a cast does: lpad(x, 5, '0') and x produce different keys, and
   285	        # anonymising the name would make them the same shape.
   286	        called = fragment[word.end() : word.end() + 1] == "("
   287	        return found if called else "?"
   288	
   289	    return _IDENTIFIER.sub(anonymous, fragment)

   294

   296	    target expression makes pairs that join to nothing, and an edge no mapping loads makes no
   297	    pairs at all. All three show up as an inherited key that is null everywhere, which reads
   298	    as data rather than as a defect. ADR 0006.

   301	        (mapping, edge) for mapping in mappings for edge in mapping.relationships

   304	    modelled = {edge.id: edge for edge in model.relationships}

   309	                f"M6 -- {model.path.name} declares {edge_id} and no mapping loads it. The "
   310	                f"engine builds no pair object at all, so every join along that edge returns "
   311	                f"null, which reads as 'these rows have no target' rather than as a gap."

   328	                f"{where}: M6 -- {edge_id} runs from {declared.source_entity_id}, and this "

   352	                f"differ, because a bare column and a cast produce different keys and the "

   234

   236	    or wrong, on rows that look like data rather than like a defect -- and none of them is

   245	            f"FROM {pairs} AS pair\nWHERE pair.rel_name = '{edge.id}'\n    AND pair.row_st = 'Y'"

   254	            f"FROM (\n"
   255	            f"    SELECT\n"

   257	            f"        pair.eff_tmstp AS observed_at\n"
   258	            f"    {open_pairs}\n"
   259	            f"    GROUP BY pair.{crossing(source.source_key)}, pair.eff_tmstp\n"
   260	            f"    HAVING count(DISTINCT pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}) > 1\n"

   271	            f"    SELECT 1\n"

   282	            f"    ON b.{target.key_column} = t.{target.key_column}\n"
   283	            f"WHERE b._stage = '{source.object_name}'\n"

     2	
     3	A slice is accepted on its presentation, so the presentation has to reach whoever accepts

    26	def _installed(kind: str, bundled: Path) -> Path | None:

    31	def _point(link: Path, target: Path) -> None:

    33	
    34	    A dangling symlink answers False to exists() and still raises on symlink_to, and this
    35	    cache outlives the image it points into.
    36	    """
    37	    if link.is_symlink() or link.exists():

    42	def shim(cache: Path, build: str, bundled: Path = BUNDLED) -> None:

    45	    if shell is not None:

    47	        target.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    48	        _point(target / "chrome-headless-shell", shell / "chrome-linux" / "headless_shell")
    49	        (target.parent / "INSTALLATION_COMPLETE").touch()
    50	
    51	    full = _installed("chromium", bundled)
    52	    if full is not None:
    53	        target = cache / f"chromium-{build}"
    54	        target.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    59	def _capture(

    72	            "--execute",
    73	            "--overwrite",
